title: Demand Shocks and Supply Shocks
short: A demand shock moves the price level and output the same way; a supply shock moves them in opposite directions.
trouble: Students expect every shock to raise prices and output together, and miss stagflation, where a negative supply shock raises prices while output falls.

blocks.html: Starting from Equilibrium and Output Gaps, any event that shifts a curve moves the economy to a new short-run equilibrium. The direction of the change depends on which curve moved.

A demand shock (AD shifts) moves the price level and real GDP in the same direction. A supply shock (SRAS shifts) moves them in opposite directions. A negative supply shock brings stagflation: a higher price level with falling output and rising unemployment.

AD slopes down and SRAS slopes up. If AD shifts right, the economy slides up along SRAS: more output, higher prices. If SRAS shifts left, the economy slides up along AD: higher prices, but less output. So the pattern of the change tells you which kind of shock hit. In the 1970s, oil price jumps raised prices while output fell, a clear supply shock.

blocks.title: Which way?
blocks.q: Starting at long-run equilibrium, a drought raises food and input costs. What happens in the short run?
steps: Higher input costs: SRAS shifts left.
Along AD, the price level rises and real GDP falls: stagflation.
blocks.a: Price level up, real GDP down

blocks.title: With equations
blocks.q: AD: $P = 180 - 5Y$ and SRAS: $P = 60 + 5Y$, so $Y = 12$, $P = 120$. Consumer confidence rises and AD becomes $P = 200 - 5Y$. Find the new equilibrium.
steps: Both rose: a demand shock moves them the same way.

blocks.html: Expecting every shock to raise prices and output together, and missing stagflation, where a negative supply shock raises prices while output falls. Check: first ask which curve shifted. Demand: same direction. Supply: opposite directions.
